name: PFC CSKA Sofia
content:
PFC CSKA Sofia is a professional football club based in Sofia and one of the most successful teams in Bulgarian football history. Founded in 1948 as part of the Central Sports Club of the Army, the club has strong historical ties to the military, which is reflected in its nickname “The Armymen.” CSKA Sofia has won a record 31 national league titles and 21 Bulgarian Cups, establishing itself as a dominant force domestically.

Internationally, CSKA Sofia has also enjoyed notable success, becoming the only Bulgarian club to reach the semi-finals of the European Cup (now the UEFA Champions League), achieving this milestone twice, as well as reaching the semi-finals of the Cup Winners’ Cup. Throughout its history, the club has been known for producing talented players and maintaining a strong presence in European competitions, particularly during the 1960s–1980s.

In modern times, CSKA Sofia continues to compete in Bulgaria’s top division, the First League, although it has faced financial and structural challenges, including a major reorganization in the 2010s. Despite these difficulties, the club remains one of the most popular and historically significant teams in Bulgaria, with a large fan base and an enduring reputation both domestically and in European football.

name: PFC Levski Sofia
content:
PFC Levski Sofia is one of the oldest and most popular football clubs in Bulgaria, based in Sofia. Founded in 1911 by students and officially registered in 1914, the club was named after Bulgarian national hero Vasil Levski. It quickly became a key figure in the development of organized football in the country, winning early regional and national titles in the 1920s–1940s and establishing a reputation as a leading club.

During the post–World War II period, Levski Sofia emerged as one of the two dominant forces in Bulgarian football, alongside its main rival CSKA Sofia. The club won multiple league titles in the late 1940s and 1950s, although it experienced fluctuations in success, including a temporary name change to Dinamo under Soviet influence before reverting to its original identity. A resurgence in the 1960s, supported by a strong youth academy and talented players, brought further domestic titles and memorable victories, solidifying its long-term prominence.

In European competitions, Levski Sofia has had notable achievements, most prominently reaching the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup Winners’ Cup and later becoming the first Bulgarian club to reach the group stage of the UEFA Champions League in 2006. In modern times, the club remains a consistent participant in Bulgaria’s top division and continues to be one of the country’s most supported teams, maintaining a strong fan base and historic legacy.

name: PFC Ludogorets Razgrad
content:
PFC Ludogorets Razgrad is a professional football club based in Razgrad, Bulgaria, founded in 1945. For much of its early history, the club played in the lower divisions and underwent several reorganizations, including mergers and periods of inactivity. Its modern rise began around 2009–2010 after restructuring, which set the foundation for rapid progress through the Bulgarian league system and eventual promotion to the top division.

The club achieved immediate and remarkable success upon reaching the top tier, winning the Bulgarian league title, the Bulgarian Cup, and the Supercup in its debut 2011–12 season—an unprecedented achievement for a newcomer. Since then, Ludogorets has dominated Bulgarian football, winning consecutive league titles and establishing itself as the country’s leading club in the 21st century. The team also holds multiple domestic trophies, including several Bulgarian Cups and a record number of Supercups.

In European competitions, Ludogorets has become one of Bulgaria’s most consistent performers. The club reached the round of 16 in the UEFA Europa League in 2013–14 and regularly participates in continental tournaments. It also became only the second Bulgarian team to reach the UEFA Champions League group stage, where it earned historic points for the country. Today, Ludogorets is known for its modern infrastructure, strong squad, and sustained success both domestically and in Europe.

name: PFC Slavia Sofia
content:
PFC Slavia Sofia is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Sofia, founded on 10 April 1913. It is considered the oldest sports club in the capital and one of the pioneers of organized football in Bulgaria. Known as “The Whites” due to their traditional colors, the club has maintained a continuous presence in the top tier of Bulgarian football for most of its history and plays its home matches at the Aleksandar Shalamanov Stadium.

Slavia enjoyed its greatest domestic success in the early and mid-20th century, winning multiple national championships between 1928 and 1943 and later adding further titles, including a notable league and cup double in the 1995–96 season. Overall, the club has won seven Bulgarian league titles and eight Bulgarian Cups, establishing itself as one of the country’s historically significant teams, even if it has not dominated as consistently as some of its rivals.

In European competitions, Slavia Sofia has achieved several notable results, most prominently reaching the semi-finals of the UEFA Cup Winners’ Cup in 1966–67 and the quarter-finals in 1981. The club also won the Balkans Cup twice in the 1980s. Despite more modest performances in recent decades, Slavia remains an important part of Bulgarian football history, with long-standing rivalries in Sofia and a reputation as a traditional and respected club.

name: PFC Cherno More Varna
content:
PFC Cherno More Varna is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Varna, founded in 1913. It is one of the oldest football institutions in the country and has spent most of its history competing in the top tier of Bulgarian football. Nicknamed “The Sailors,” the club takes its name from the Black Sea and plays its home matches at Stadion Ticha.

The club’s modern identity was shaped in 1959 after a merger that led to the adoption of the name Cherno More. During the communist era, like many Bulgarian teams, it underwent multiple reorganizations, name changes, and structural shifts imposed by the state. Despite these challenges, Cherno More remained a consistent presence in the top division, occasionally achieving strong league finishes and memorable international friendlies, including a notable win over Ajax in 1966.

In the post-1990 period, Cherno More experienced financial difficulties and spells in the second division but later re-established itself in Bulgaria’s First League. The club is considered one of the most competitive teams outside the capital Sofia, highlighted by winning the Bulgarian Cup in 2015 and maintaining regular top-half finishes in recent years. Today, it continues to be a stable and respected presence in Bulgarian football.

name: FC Lokomotiv 1929 Sofia
content:
FC Lokomotiv 1929 Sofia is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Sofia, founded in 1929 as Railway Sports Club. Nicknamed “The Railwaymen,” the club has strong historical ties to railway workers and has spent most of its existence competing in the top tier of Bulgarian football. Lokomotiv plays its home matches at Stadion Lokomotiv and is considered one of the traditional clubs in the capital.

The club enjoyed its greatest success in the 20th century, winning four Bulgarian league titles and four Bulgarian Cups. Lokomotiv established itself as a competitive force domestically, particularly during the 1930s–1970s, and also had notable performances in European competitions, including appearances in the European Cup and UEFA tournaments. It was known for strong squads and historic victories, such as high-scoring matches in continental competitions.

In modern times, the club faced serious financial difficulties, leading to bankruptcy and dissolution in 2015. A new entity, FC Lokomotiv 1929 Sofia, was subsequently formed and is regarded as a successor, although not officially recognized as the same legal club by the Bulgarian Football Union. Since then, Lokomotiv has worked its way back into the top division and continues to compete in Bulgaria’s First League, maintaining its historical identity and legacy within Bulgarian football.

name: FC Lovech
content:
FC Lovech is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Lovech, with origins dating back to 1921 when it was founded as Hisarya Sports Club. Over the decades, the club underwent numerous name changes—including Karpachev, Osam, and LEX—reflecting political and economic shifts in Bulgaria. For much of the 20th century, it competed mainly in the second division, gradually building a stable presence in national football.

A major turning point came in the early 1990s, when private sponsorship led to improved performances and promotion to the top tier for the first time in the club’s history in 1994. Although its initial stay in the top division was short-lived, this period marked the beginning of greater ambitions and development. In later years, under the identity of Litex Lovech, the club achieved significant success, including multiple Bulgarian league titles and cup victories, becoming one of the strongest teams in the country during the late 1990s and 2000s.

In recent years, the club has undergone major structural and identity changes. Ownership returned to the local municipality in 2024, and the team reverted to the name FC Lovech. However, financial and sporting difficulties followed, including relegation and the loss of its professional license in 2026, effectively leading to the club’s dissolution. Despite this, FC Lovech remains historically important in Bulgarian football due to its long history and its successful era as Litex Lovech.

name: Botev Plovdiv
content:
PFC Botev Plovdiv is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Plovdiv, founded in 1912 by students and named after national hero Hristo Botev. It is widely regarded as one of the oldest football clubs in Bulgaria and has played an important role in the development of the sport in the country. The club achieved early success by winning its first national championship in 1929, becoming the first team from Plovdiv to claim the Bulgarian title.

Throughout its history, Botev Plovdiv experienced numerous name changes and reorganizations, particularly during the communist era, when it was known under different identities such as DNV, DNA, and Trakia. Despite these changes, the club remained a regular participant in the top division and maintained a strong football tradition. It enjoyed periods of competitiveness, including strong league finishes and domestic cup runs, while continuing to develop notable Bulgarian players.

In the modern era, Botev Plovdiv has faced financial challenges, including administrative relegation in 2010 due to debts, but has since re-established itself in Bulgarian top-flight football. The club continues to compete domestically and participate in European competitions, with appearances in tournaments such as the UEFA Europa League and UEFA Conference League qualifiers. Today, it remains one of Bulgaria’s historic and well-supported clubs, with a passionate fan base and a significant legacy in national football.

name: FC Spartak Varna
content:
FC Spartak Varna is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Varna, with origins dating back to 1918 when it was founded as SC Sokol. Over the years, the club underwent several mergers and name changes, including becoming Spartak Varna in 1945 after uniting with other local teams. It is one of the traditional clubs in the city and has a long-standing presence in Bulgarian football, although much of its history has been spent moving between divisions.

Spartak Varna achieved its greatest success in the early 20th century, winning the Bulgarian championship in 1932 under the name Shipchenski Sokol. The club has also reached the Bulgarian Cup final twice and has participated in several European competitions, including becoming the first Bulgarian team to play in the European Cup Winners’ Cup in 1961–62. Despite these highlights, Spartak has generally not been among the dominant forces in Bulgarian football.

In recent years, the club has experienced financial difficulties and structural changes, including the founding of a new entity in 2015 and a merger with Spartak 1918 in 2017. After rebuilding in the lower divisions, Spartak returned to the top tier in 2022 after a long absence but struggled to remain there and was relegated again shortly after. Today, the club continues to compete in Bulgaria’s professional leagues while maintaining its historical identity and local support.

name: PFC Lokomotiv Plovdiv
content:
PFC Lokomotiv Plovdiv is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Plovdiv, founded in 1926. The club emerged from the merger of local teams and developed a strong identity connected to railway workers, which is reflected in its nickname “The Smurfs” and its traditional black-and-white colors. Lokomotiv plays its home matches at Stadion Lokomotiv (Lauta) and is one of the well-established clubs in Bulgarian football history.

Throughout its history, Lokomotiv has experienced multiple reorganizations, especially during the communist era, but remained a stable presence in Bulgarian top-flight football. The club’s greatest achievement came in the 2003–04 season when it won its first and only Bulgarian First League title, finishing ahead of Levski Sofia. It also won the Bulgarian Supercup in 2004 and has achieved several strong league finishes and domestic cup runs.

In European competitions, Lokomotiv Plovdiv has regularly participated in UEFA tournaments, including the Champions League and Europa League qualifiers, but with limited progress on the continental stage. The club is known for its passionate fan base and strong local rivalry with Botev Plovdiv, with their matches forming one of the most intense derbies in Bulgarian football. Today, Lokomotiv remains a consistent First League team with a solid reputation in domestic football.

name: PFC Spartak Plovdiv
content:
PFC Spartak Plovdiv is a Bulgarian football club based in Plovdiv, founded in 1947 after the merger of three local teams. The club’s name “Spartak” refers to Spartacus, which is why its supporters are nicknamed “The Gladiators.” It has traditionally played its home matches at Stadion Todor Diev and has spent most of its history moving between the top and lower divisions of Bulgarian football.

The club experienced its strongest period in the 1950s and 1960s, when it competed in Bulgaria’s top division and achieved its main honours. Spartak Plovdiv won the Bulgarian league title once in the 1962–63 season and also secured the Bulgarian Cup in 1958. During this era, it also participated in European competitions, including appearances in the European Cup, marking the peak of its sporting success.

In later decades, Spartak Plovdiv gradually declined from its top-tier status, spending much of its time in lower divisions and facing financial instability. The club was eventually dissolved in 2016 but was re-established a year later, continuing to compete in the Bulgarian football pyramid, mainly in the lower leagues. Despite its struggles, Spartak remains a historically important club in Plovdiv with a loyal local following and a legacy tied to its early successes.

name: PFC Beroe Stara Zagora
content:
PFC Beroe Stara Zagora is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Stara Zagora, founded in 1916. The club was formed through early mergers of local teams and has become one of the main representatives of the city in national football. Beroe plays its home matches at Stadion Beroe and is traditionally associated with the green-and-white colors, earning the nickname “The Greens.” It is considered one of the historic clubs in Bulgaria, with a long-standing presence in the country’s football system.

The club’s most successful period came in the mid-to-late 20th century. Beroe won its first and only Bulgarian league title in 1986, marking the peak of its domestic achievements. It also enjoyed strong performances in regional competitions, becoming one of the most successful Bulgarian teams in the Balkans Cup with four titles. Additionally, the club recorded notable European results, including victories against teams like Juventus and Athletic Bilbao in the 1970s.

In modern times, Beroe has remained a regular participant in Bulgaria’s First League but has faced financial and organizational instability, leading to ownership changes and restructuring. Despite these challenges, the club continues to compete at the top level and is known for its resilience and ability to rebuild. Its legacy is defined by its historic 1986 championship, strong regional success, and memorable European performances, making it an important part of Bulgarian football history.

name: PFC Septemvri Sofia
content:
PFC Septemvri Sofia is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Sofia, founded on 5 November 1944 through the merger of several local teams. The club’s name refers to the September 1944 political changes in Bulgaria, and it has traditionally been associated with developing players through its youth academy. Septemvri has spent much of its history moving between the top two divisions of Bulgarian football, without long-term stability in the top tier.

Historically, the club’s most notable achievement came in 1960 when it won the Bulgarian Cup and also finished strongly in the league during the same period. Septemvri has been especially recognized for its youth development system, which has produced many players who later moved on to stronger Bulgarian and international clubs. Over time, it became known more as a “development club” rather than a consistent title contender.

In modern football, Septemvri Sofia has continued to fluctuate between divisions, including recent promotions back to the Bulgarian First League. The club has changed ownership and structure in recent years, but it remains active in professional football and maintains its focus on developing young talent. Despite limited major trophies, it holds a stable place in Bulgarian football due to its academy tradition and long history.

name: SFC Etar Veliko Tarnovo
content:
SFC Etar Veliko Tarnovo is a Bulgarian football club based in Veliko Tarnovo, with its origins connected to the historic club FC Etar, which was originally founded in 1924 through the merger of several local teams. The original Etar became one of the important provincial clubs in Bulgaria and reached its peak in the late 1980s and early 1990s, including winning the Bulgarian championship in the 1990–91 season. However, due to financial problems, the historic club was dissolved in 2003, leading to a series of successor teams.

After the dissolution, several re-foundations and successor projects followed, including Etar 1924 and later SFC Etar Veliko Tarnovo, which emerged in 2013 as a continuation of football tradition in the city. These new versions started from the lower divisions and gradually rebuilt their place in Bulgarian football. Despite not being the original 1924 legal entity, they are widely seen as carrying the legacy and identity of the historic Etar club, including its nickname “The Bolyars.”

In modern times, SFC Etar competes mainly in Bulgaria’s second tier, with occasional promotions to the First League. The club plays its home matches at Stadion Ivaylo and continues to develop as a stable regional team. Although it has not yet reached the historical success of the original Etar, it remains an important representative of Veliko Tarnovo football tradition and its long-established fan base.

name: FC CSKA 1948 Sofia
content:
FC CSKA 1948 Sofia is a Bulgarian professional football club based in Sofia, founded on 19 July 2016. It was created by supporters and figures associated with the historical CSKA identity, following disputes around the restructuring and ownership changes of the original CSKA Sofia. The club started from the lowest tiers of Bulgarian football and was built as a separate project, aiming to rise through the league system in a “from the ground up” way.

After its formation, CSKA 1948 progressed rapidly through the Bulgarian football pyramid, winning successive promotions from the lower amateur divisions to reach the professional leagues. By 2020, the club had already secured promotion to Bulgaria’s top division, the First League, after winning the Second League. In the following seasons, it established itself as a competitive top-flight team, even achieving strong league finishes and reaching the Bulgarian Cup final in the early 2020s.

In European football, CSKA 1948 made its debut in UEFA competitions after finishing high in the domestic league, earning qualification for the UEFA Europa Conference League. The club plays its home matches at Stadion Bistritsa and is known for its relatively young structure compared to traditional Bulgarian clubs. Despite its short history, it has become part of the modern football landscape in Bulgaria, contributing to the ongoing rivalry and identity debate around the CSKA name in Sofia.

name: Velbazhd Kyustendil
content:
Velbazhd Kyustendil is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Kyustendil, originally founded in 1919. Throughout its long history, the club has gone through numerous name changes and reorganisations, but it is generally seen as the continuation of the city’s early football tradition. For most of its existence, Velbazhd has competed in the lower and second tiers of Bulgarian football, slowly building its reputation as a strong provincial side.

The club’s most successful period came in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when it established itself in Bulgaria’s top division. Velbazhd achieved its best league results by finishing 3rd in the A Group for three consecutive seasons (1998–2001), marking a historic peak for the club. During this time, it also reached the Bulgarian Cup final in 2001 and participated in European competition via the Intertoto Cup, highlighting its brief but strong golden era.

However, after the 2000–01 season, the club’s top-flight project effectively ended when owner Georgi Iliev merged Velbazhd with Lokomotiv Plovdiv. This move transferred most key players and resources to Plovdiv, and Velbazhd ceased to exist at the highest level of Bulgarian football, later being re-established from the lower divisions. Today, the club continues in various forms within the lower leagues, preserving its identity and tradition in Kyustendil while never fully returning to its late-1990s peak.

name: PFC Neftochimic Burgas
content:
PFC Neftochimic Burgas is a Bulgarian football club based in Burgas, originally founded in 1962 by workers of the local oil refinery, which also inspired the club’s name. The team began its development in the lower regional leagues under the name Stroitel before being renamed Neftochimic in 1964. It is closely linked to the industrial identity of the city and the petroleum industry, which shaped both its early structure and long-term support base.

The club’s rise to prominence came in the 1990s, when it reached Bulgaria’s top division for the first time and quickly established itself as a competitive side. Neftochimic achieved strong league performances, including a 4th-place finish and a Bulgarian Professional League Cup victory in the mid-1990s, as well as participating in European competitions. During this period, it became one of the more successful provincial clubs in Bulgarian football.

However, the club later faced serious financial instability, leading to multiple restructurings, rebrandings, and periods of dissolution and reformation. After being dissolved in 2009, Neftochimic was re-established and has since fluctuated between divisions, including spells in the top flight and lower regional leagues. Today, it continues to exist as a reformed club representing Burgas, maintaining its identity and legacy despite its turbulent modern history.

name: FC Marek Dupnitsa
content:
FC Marek Dupnitsa is a Bulgarian football club based in Dupnitsa, founded in 1915 through the unification of several early local teams. The club has a long and complex history, with multiple reorganisations and name changes before becoming known as Marek. It is traditionally associated with the “Bonchuk” Stadium and is considered one of the most historic provincial clubs in Bulgaria.

Marek’s most successful period came in the 1970s, when the club achieved its best-ever league performances, including finishing 3rd in the Bulgarian top division and winning the Bulgarian Cup in 1978. During this golden era, Marek also competed in European competitions and produced some of its most famous results, establishing itself briefly as one of the strongest sides outside the capital Sofia.

In later decades, the club experienced instability, moving frequently between divisions and facing financial and administrative issues, including relegations and re-foundations. Despite these setbacks, Marek continued to rebuild and return to professional football at different points, most recently competing in Bulgaria’s Second League. Today, it remains an important traditional club with strong local identity and a history tied closely to Bulgarian football’s provincial heritage.

name: PFC Akademik Sofia
content:
PFC Akademik Sofia is a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded in 1947 by students from Sofia University. The club quickly developed into a competitive side and made its debut in the top division (A Group) in 1949. Known by the nickname “The Students,” Akademik is closely associated with academic life and education, which shaped its identity and early development.

During the 1950s and again in the 1970s, Akademik experienced its strongest periods in Bulgarian football. The club achieved notable league finishes, including 3rd place in 1950 and 1975–76, and reached the Bulgarian Cup final in 1951. It also enjoyed international success by winning the Balkans Cup in 1974 and later competing in UEFA competitions, including memorable matches against strong European teams such as AC Milan.

After its golden era, Akademik spent long periods outside the top division, particularly between 1982 and 2010, and struggled with financial instability in modern times. The club briefly returned to the A Group in the 2010–11 season but was relegated again and eventually dissolved in 2012 due to financial problems. A successor club, Akademik 1947 Sofia, was later formed, but it is considered a separate legal entity and does not continue the original records.

name: POFC Botev Vratsa
content:
POFC Botev Vratsa is a Bulgarian football club based in Vratsa, founded in 1921. The club represents one of the traditional teams from the Bulgarian provinces and is nicknamed “The Green Lions.” It plays its home matches at Stadion Hristo Botev and has spent most of its history competing between the top two divisions of Bulgarian football.

Botev Vratsa experienced its strongest period during the late 1960s and 1970s. The club’s greatest achievement came in the 1970–71 season when it finished third in Bulgaria’s top division, which remains its best league result. During this era, Botev also established itself as a stable First League team and participated in European competitions, including the UEFA Cup in the early 1970s.

After 1990, the club entered a long period of decline, spending many seasons outside the top flight due to relegations and financial difficulties. However, Botev has repeatedly managed to return to the First League in the 21st century, including promotions in 2011 and 2018. Today, it remains a regular participant in Bulgarian top-flight football, known for its resilience and strong local support.

name: OFC Spartak Pleven
content:
OFC Spartak Pleven is a Bulgarian football club based in Pleven, founded in 1919 by Dragomir Nestorov and a group of local students. In its early years, the club went through several name changes, including Skobelov, Belite Orli, and Republikanec, before finally becoming Spartak Pleven in 1946 after opposition from supporters to political renaming. It is considered one of the traditional provincial clubs in Bulgarian football, with a long history tied to the city of Pleven.

Spartak Pleven experienced its strongest period in the mid-20th century. The club achieved its best league result in 1958, finishing 3rd in the Bulgarian top division, and also reached the Bulgarian Cup final in 1957. During later decades, it spent multiple seasons in the top flight and second tier, with several promotions and relegations shaping its competitive history.

In modern times, Spartak Pleven has mostly competed in Bulgaria’s lower divisions, but it has continued to rebuild and occasionally return to the professional levels. The club remains an important football symbol for the city of Pleven, with a long-standing identity and history of producing notable players and memorable cup runs.

name: FC Spartak Sofia
content:
FC Spartak Sofia is a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded in 1947 through the merger of several local teams, including Rakovski and FK-13. The club quickly became part of the national football system and played for many years in Bulgaria’s top division. Its traditional colours were blue and white, and it was known for its home ground, Rakovski Stadium.

During the 1950s and 1960s, Spartak Sofia reached its strongest period. The club finished as runner-up in the Bulgarian championship twice (1951 and 1952) and won the Bulgarian Cup in 1968, which remains its most important trophy. It also reached the final of the Balkans Cup in the 1967–68 season, marking its brief presence in regional European competition.

In 1969, Spartak Sofia was merged into Levski Sofia, which ended its independent existence for a period, although it was later restored and continued in various forms. The club eventually struggled with instability and was dissolved in 2007. Despite this, Spartak remains part of Sofia’s football history, remembered as a traditional side that contributed to Bulgarian football in the mid-20th century.

name: Sportist Sofia
content:
Sportist Sofia was a football club founded in the “Hadji Dimitar” district of Sofia, originally starting as a section of SK Shipka before becoming an independent club in 1936. It quickly rose through the Bulgarian football system, reaching the Third Sofia Division in 1938 and the First Division by 1942. Despite very limited financial resources, no home stadium, and a squad made mostly of local players from the neighbourhood, the club built a surprisingly strong team and developed a talented generation of footballers.

During World War II, Sportist achieved its peak performance. In 1943, it reached the quarter-finals of the national championship, where it was narrowly eliminated by future champions Slavia Sofia. The club continued to grow and in 1945 reached the national championship final. There, Sportist defeated Levski Sofia in the quarter-finals and Spartak Varna in the semi-finals before losing the final to Lokomotiv Sofia over two legs, with star striker Stefan Bozhkov scoring both goals for the team in the final.

After this golden period, financial problems led to the departure of key players, and the club gradually weakened. Eventually, Sportist was merged with other teams during the reorganisation of Bulgarian football in 1949, disappearing under the name “Sredets” and later becoming part of state-controlled sports structures. Decades later, the club was revived in 2021 as “Sportist 13 Sofia,” starting again from the lower amateur divisions and continuing its modern existence while referencing its historic roots and original founding tradition.

name: SK Vladislav
content:
SK Vladislav was a Bulgarian football club from Varna, founded on 3 April 1916 under the name “Napred.” After several early name changes and administrative issues, the club was officially established as SK Vladislav in 1921. It became one of the key football teams in Varna during the interwar period and developed a strong squad that quickly rose to national prominence.

In the 1920s and 1930s, Vladislav became one of the most successful clubs in Bulgaria, winning the national championship three times (1925, 1926, and 1934). It also played several important finals against top Sofia teams such as Levski and Slavia, establishing itself as a major force in early Bulgarian football. Its success was built on strong local talent and early tactical development, making it one of the dominant teams of its era.

In the 1920s and 1930s, Vladislav became one of the most successful clubs in Bulgaria, winning the national championship three times (1925, 1926, and 1934). It also played several important finals against top Sofia teams such as Levski and Slavia, establishing itself as a major force in early Bulgarian football. Its success was built on strong local talent and early tactical development, making it one of the dominant teams of its era.

name: Atletik-Slava 1923
content:
OSK AS-23 (Officers’ Sports Club Athletic–Slava 1923) was a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded on 28 October 1923 through the merger of three local teams: Athletic Sofia, Slava Sofia, and the Officers’ Sports Club. The club was closely linked to the Bulgarian military and used the stadium that later became the site of the modern Bulgarian Army Stadium. It played an important role in early Sofia football and was considered one of the stronger teams of its era.

AS-23 achieved significant success in the interwar period. The club won the Bulgarian national championship in 1931 and also claimed the Bulgarian Cup in 1941. During the 1930s and early 1940s, it regularly competed at the top level of Bulgarian football and built a reputation as one of the strongest army-associated teams in the country.

AS-23 achieved significant success in the interwar period. The club won the Bulgarian national championship in 1931 and also claimed the Bulgarian Cup in 1941. During the 1930s and early 1940s, it regularly competed at the top level of Bulgarian football and built a reputation as one of the strongest army-associated teams in the country.

name: Sportklub Sofia
content:
Sportklub Sofia was a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded in 1912 originally under the name SC Karavelov. It was created in the Tri Kladentsi district and later renamed Sportklub Sofia after several early reorganisations, including a short merger with Slavia Sofia in 1919–1920 before becoming independent again. The club gradually developed into one of the stronger sides in the early Sofia football scene and participated in the city’s first organised competitions.

Sportklub Sofia was a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded in 1912 originally under the name SC Karavelov. It was created in the Tri Kladentsi district and later renamed Sportklub Sofia after several early reorganisations, including a short merger with Slavia Sofia in 1919–1920 before becoming independent again. The club gradually developed into one of the stronger sides in the early Sofia football scene and participated in the city’s first organised competitions.

After the political changes in 1944, Sportklub Sofia was dissolved and merged with other clubs (Sokol Sofia and Vazrazhdane Sofia), forming Septemvri Sofia on its base. This marked the end of Sportklub as an independent entity, but its legacy continued through its successor clubs. Today, it is remembered as one of the early historic teams of Sofia, notable mainly for its 1935 championship and its role in the development of Bulgarian football in the capital.

name: SK Ticha
content:
SK Ticha was a Bulgarian football club based in Varna, founded on 3 March 1913 under the original name “Galata.” It later merged with Sportist in 1914 and was renamed SK Ticha in 1919, becoming one of the leading football teams in the city of Varna during the interwar period. The club developed early success and became an important part of the growing football culture in Bulgaria’s coastal region.

During the 1930s, Ticha experienced its strongest period, achieving major national success. The club finished as runners-up in the Bulgarian championship in 1935 and 1936 before winning its first and only national title in the 1937–38 season. This made Ticha one of the strongest Bulgarian teams of its era, regularly competing with top clubs from Sofia and establishing itself among the national elite.

During the 1930s, Ticha experienced its strongest period, achieving major national success. The club finished as runners-up in the Bulgarian championship in 1935 and 1936 before winning its first and only national title in the 1937–38 season. This made Ticha one of the strongest Bulgarian teams of its era, regularly competing with top clubs from Sofia and establishing itself among the national elite.

name: FC Dunav Ruse
content:
FC Dunav Ruse is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Ruse, founded on 16 February 1949 through the merger of several local teams, including Dinamo and Rusenets. The club takes its name from the Danube River and is commonly nicknamed “The Dragons.” It was created as part of a broader reorganization of sports in the city and gradually became the main football representative of Ruse.

Throughout its history, Dunav has mostly competed between Bulgaria’s top and second tiers, with multiple spells in the First League during different eras. The club’s notable achievements include finishing 4th in the top division in 1975, 1989, and 2017, as well as reaching several Bulgarian Cup finals in the early and mid-20th century. One of its most successful modern periods came in the 2010s, when it returned to the top flight and again reached European qualification positions.

Dunav has also experienced financial instability and periods of decline, including relegations and temporary withdrawal from professional competition in the early 2010s. The club was later re-established and rebuilt from the lower divisions, eventually returning to professional football. Today, FC Dunav Ruse continues to compete in Bulgaria’s second tier, maintaining its identity as one of the traditional football clubs from northern Bulgaria.

name: Gragjanski Skopje
content:
Gragjanski Skopje was a football club from Skopje, founded in 1922 under the name FC Citizens Skopje. In its early development it quickly became one of the most important clubs in the city, and in 1926 it merged with FC Vardar and moved to Vardar’s ground in the City Park. From that point, the club became a regular participant in the Yugoslav football system and later in regional competitions organized in the Skopje area.

During the late 1920s and 1930s, Gragjanski established itself as the strongest club from the Vardar Banovina region. It competed in the Skopje Football Subassociation and later reached higher levels of Yugoslav football, even taking part in the Royal League system. The club won several regional championships and had its best domestic form in the late 1930s, when it was considered one of the most competitive teams outside the major Yugoslav centers.

In 1941, during World War II, the club was effectively transformed due to political and territorial changes, as the region came under Bulgarian administration. Gragjanski merged with several local clubs to form FK Makedonia, which competed in the Bulgarian championship during the war years. After the war ended, the club went through further mergers, eventually contributing to the creation of FK Vardar in 1947, ending Gragjanski’s independent existence but leaving a lasting legacy in Skopje football history.

name: FC Shipka Sofia
content:
FC Shipka Sofia was a Bulgarian football club based in Sofia, founded on 2 May 1923 after a merger of local amateur teams. Initially created under the name FC Sparta, the club was renamed Shipka in 1924 in honour of the historic Shipka Pass. It quickly developed within the Sofia football system and became part of the competitive city leagues during the interwar period.

In the late 1930s, Shipka rose to the national level and competed in the Bulgarian State Football Championship for several seasons. The club’s greatest achievement came in 1939 when it won the Bulgarian Cup, marking its peak in domestic football. During this period, Shipka established itself as a solid mid-tier team capable of competing against stronger Sofia clubs, even if it never became a consistent title contender.

In 1944, following major political and structural changes in Bulgarian sport after World War II, FC Shipka Sofia was dissolved and merged with AS-23 to form FC Chavdar Sofia, a predecessor of CSKA Sofia. This marked the end of Shipka as an independent club, but its legacy continued indirectly through later reorganisations and successor teams within Sofia football history.

name: FC Levski Ruse
content:
Levski (Ruse) was a Bulgarian football club founded in 1922 as part of a third football unit within SK Sava (Ruse). The team initially played at the Napredak ground and was financially supported by local patron D. Dyulgerov. It developed in the interwar football structure of Ruse and gradually became one of the strongest clubs in the city, building a reputation as a competitive provincial side.

The club’s golden era came between 1934 and 1940, when it became one of the leading teams in Bulgarian football outside Sofia. Levski Ruse achieved its greatest success in 1937 by finishing as runner-up in the Bulgarian national championship, the highest achievement in the history of men’s football in the city. During this period, it also regularly competed in the national cup finals, won multiple city championships, and participated in the National Football Division, while producing several players who represented Bulgaria internationally.

After its peak, the club was heavily penalized and removed from the national league system in 1940, leading to its disbandment. It was later reactivated and went through several reorganisations, including a merger with Angel Kanchev in 1944 and eventual absorption into Dynamo Ruse in 1946, which itself became part of the formation of modern FC Dunav in 1949. A formal split from Dunav occurred again in 2005, but the original Levski (Ruse) entity no longer exists as an independent top-level club, remaining only as part of the historical football heritage of the city.

name: FK 13 Sofia
content:
FK 13 Sofia was a Bulgarian football club based in the capital city Sofia, founded in 1913 by a group of students and originally known as “Sava.” It became officially established as FK 13 Sofia in the same year and is considered one of the early pioneers of club football in Bulgaria. The team was nicknamed “The Veterans” due to its long tradition and early role in the development of organized football in the country. It was based in central Sofia and drew its identity from educated and professional members of society, including lawyers, doctors, and military students.

During the interwar period, FK 13 became one of the stronger Bulgarian teams, competing regularly in national competitions and achieving notable success. The club won the Bulgarian Cup twice, in 1938 and 1940, and also participated in the national championship system, where it recorded solid mid-table and upper-tier finishes. One of its most important achievements came in 1938 when it won the first edition of the Tsar’s Cup, marking a historic moment in Bulgarian football history.

In 1944, after major political changes in Bulgaria, FK 13 Sofia was dissolved and merged into Rakovski Sofia, ending its independent existence. Rakovski later became part of further reorganisations that eventually contributed to the formation of Spartak Sofia. Today, FK 13 is remembered as one of the founding-era clubs of Bulgarian football, notable for its early influence, cup successes, and contribution to the development of the sport in Sofia.

name: FC Sliven
content:
FC Sliven is a Bulgarian football club from the city of Sliven, with its football tradition dating back to 1914 when the first local team “Sportist” was founded. Over the decades, the club evolved through many reorganisations and name changes, including Asenovets, DNA, General Zaimov, and Mlada Gvardia, before becoming FC Sliven in the 1960s. It became the main representative of football in the city and established itself as a stable participant in Bulgaria’s national competitions.

The club’s strongest period came between the mid-1970s and early 1990s, when it spent many consecutive seasons in Bulgaria’s top division. Its peak achievement was in the 1983–84 season, when Sliven finished 3rd in the league and qualified for European competition for the first time. The club’s greatest trophy success came in 1990, when it won the Bulgarian Cup after defeating CSKA Sofia in the final, which marked the highest point in its history.

After the early 1990s, FC Sliven entered a period of decline due to financial problems and successive relegations, eventually leading to bankruptcy and disappearance from professional football. The club was later re-founded as OFC Sliven 2000 in 2000, continuing the football tradition of the city but as a new legal entity. Since then, Sliven has moved between divisions and lower tiers, remaining an active but unstable presence in Bulgarian football.

name: OFC Pirin Blagoevgrad
content:
OFC Pirin Blagoevgrad is a Bulgarian football club based in Blagoevgrad, with origins tracing back to 1922, when the first Pirin team was founded. The club takes its name from the Pirin mountain range and is nicknamed “The Eagles.” It plays its home matches at Stadion Hristo Botev and has long been considered one of the key football representatives of southwestern Bulgaria.

Throughout its history, Pirin has spent many seasons moving between Bulgaria’s top division and lower leagues, but it is especially known for its role as a strong player-development club. The team has reached four Bulgarian Cup finals but has not won the trophy, and it has also competed in European tournaments such as the UEFA Cup and Cup Winners’ Cup. In its strongest periods, Pirin produced notable results in the First League and developed a reputation for competitive performances against the country’s top clubs.

In modern times, the club has undergone several reorganisations, mergers, and financial restructurings, including periods of bankruptcy and re-founding. Despite instability, OFC Pirin continues to compete professionally in Bulgaria’s league system, most recently alternating between the First and Second Leagues. Today, it remains an important regional club, valued especially for its academy and its contribution to Bulgarian football talent development.

name: FC Arda Kardzhali
content:
FC Arda Kardzhali is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Kardzhali, founded on 10 August 1924 under the name Rodopski Sokol. The club later adopted the name Arda, inspired by the nearby Arda River, and spent most of its early history fluctuating between the second and third tiers of Bulgarian football. In 2013, the original club was dissolved due to financial problems after years of instability.

The club was re-established in 2015 and began rebuilding from the regional leagues. After rapid progress and new investment in 2017, Arda quickly climbed through the divisions and reached the Bulgarian First League for the first time in its history in 2019. This rise marked a major turning point, transforming Arda into a stable top-flight team and establishing it as a modern football project in Bulgaria.

Since reaching the elite level, Arda has achieved its best results in the 2020s, including a historic run to the Bulgarian Cup final in 2021 and qualification for European competitions for the first time. The club plays its home matches at Arena Arda, a modern stadium in Kardzhali, and has become a consistent First League side, representing one of the fastest modern rises in Bulgarian football.

name: PFC Montana
content:
PFC Montana is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Montana, founded on 20 March 1921. The club was originally created as SC Hristo Mihaylov through the merger of several early local sports groups, and it went through numerous reorganisations and name changes during the 20th century. Over time, it became the main football representative of the city and gradually built a stable presence in Bulgarian professional football.

Throughout its history, Montana has mostly competed between the top two divisions of Bulgarian football, with several spells in the First League. The club’s early decades were marked by constant restructuring, but it established itself more firmly in the professional system from the 1990s onward. One of its strongest early modern periods came in the mid-1990s when it first reached the top division and achieved a solid mid-table presence, while also developing players who later moved to bigger Bulgarian clubs.

In the 21st century, Montana has become a typical “yo-yo” club, moving between the First and Second Leagues. It reached its peak modern achievement by reaching the Bulgarian Cup final in the 2015–16 season and has since continued to fluctuate between divisions, including recent promotions back to the top flight. The club plays its home matches at Ogosta Stadium and remains an important representative of northwestern Bulgarian football tradition.

name: OFC Pomorie
content:
OFC Pomorie is a Bulgarian football club based in the coastal town of Pomorie, founded in 1934. The team represents a long local football tradition that began with several earlier reorganisations and name changes before stabilising under its current municipal structure. It plays its home matches at the Pomorie Stadium, a small modern venue with a capacity of about 2,000 spectators.

Throughout its history, Pomorie has mostly competed in the lower and second tiers of Bulgarian football, but it has had several strong periods. The club reached one of its most successful modern phases in the early 2010s, when it earned promotion to the Second League and even finished as runners-up twice at that level. It also achieved a remarkable run in the 2009–10 Bulgarian Cup, reaching the final, which remains its greatest achievement in national competitions.

In recent years, OFC Pomorie has experienced financial difficulties, leading to relegation and withdrawal from higher professional divisions after the 2019–20 season. The club continues to exist at an amateur or regional level, maintaining its football tradition in the Burgas region. Despite its instability, Pomorie remains a recognizable name in Bulgarian football due to its cup final appearance and periods of strong second-division performance.

name: FC Chernomorets Burgas
content:
FC Chernomorets Burgas is a Bulgarian football club from the city of Burgas with origins dating back to 1919, when the original sports organisation SC Chernomorets was formed from earlier local clubs. Over the decades, the club went through multiple reorganisations, name changes (including FC Lyuboslav and SC Botev during the communist period), and structural reforms, but remained one of the main football representatives of the Black Sea city.

The club’s most successful period came mainly in the late 1970s and 1980s, when it established itself as a stable First League side in Bulgaria. Chernomorets spent many seasons in the top division, with its best league performances including high mid-table finishes in the early 1980s. A major highlight came in 1989, when the club reached the Bulgarian Cup final and later participated in the UEFA Cup Winners’ Cup, marking its peak on the national and European stage.

After the early 1990s, the club experienced financial instability and decline, leading to relegations and eventual bankruptcy in 2006, which resulted in its dissolution. In the following years, successor projects such as PSFC Chernomorets Burgas and later Chernomorets 1919 were created to continue the football tradition in Burgas. Today, the name “Chernomorets” remains active through re-founded clubs, preserving the legacy of one of the city’s most historically significant football institutions.

name: FC Chirpan
content:
FC Chirpan is a Bulgarian football club based in the town of Chirpan, founded in 1929 originally under the name “Yavorov.” It was later restructured and took its current name FC Chirpan in 1981. The club developed as a local team in southern Bulgaria and mainly competed in the regional and lower national divisions, representing the town in the Bulgarian football system.

The club’s most notable sporting achievement came in 1983, when, while playing in the second division (B Group), it reached the final of the Cup of the Soviet Army. This was a historic moment for the club, although it lost the final 3–1 to Lokomotiv Plovdiv. This run remains the peak of Chirpan’s competitive success and the most significant result in its history.

In modern times, FC Chirpan has remained active mostly in the lower tiers of Bulgarian football, competing in regional leagues and amateur divisions. The club continues to play at Yavorov Stadium and represents a traditional small-town football side with a long local history, though it has never returned to the higher levels of Bulgarian football since its brief peak in the 1980s.

name: FC Dorostol Silistra
content:
FC Dorostol Silistra is a Bulgarian football club based in the city of Silistra, with origins traditionally traced back to 1902 through early school-based sports activity, although the club was officially founded in 1945. It developed through several reorganisations in the city’s football structure and became the main representative team of Silistra. Dorostol plays its home matches at the Louis Eyer Stadium and is known for its blue and white colours, maintaining a long-standing local football tradition in the region.

Throughout its history, Dorostol has mostly competed in the lower tiers of Bulgarian football, but it has had moments of success, including spells in the second division and occasional strong cup performances. One of its most notable achievements came in 1984, when the club reached the final of the Cup of the Soviet Army, where it was defeated by Levski Sofia. This run remains the club’s greatest competitive highlight at national level.

In modern times, FC Dorostol has experienced financial instability and multiple dissolutions and re-formations, including a re-establishment phase in the 2010s. The club continues to participate in the lower leagues of Bulgarian football, most recently competing in the North-East Third League. Despite its fluctuations, Dorostol remains an important symbol of football in Silistra and retains its historical identity as one of the oldest football traditions in Bulgaria.

name: FC Minyor Radnevo
content:
FC Minyor Radnevo is a Bulgarian football club based in the town of Radnevo, founded in 1952. The club was created during the post-war restructuring of Bulgarian sports and is closely connected to the local mining industry, which also inspired its name “Minyor” (“Miner”). It represents one of the typical industrial-town teams in Bulgaria and has mainly competed in the lower divisions of the national football system.

Throughout its history, Minyor Radnevo has mostly played in the regional leagues and the third tier of Bulgarian football, with occasional appearances in higher divisions. One of its most notable sporting achievements came in 1989, when the club reached the final of the Cup of the Soviet Army, marking its peak moment in national competition. Despite limited resources and small-scale infrastructure, the club has remained a stable presence in South-East Bulgarian football.

In modern times, FC Minyor Radnevo continues to compete in the South-East Third League, maintaining its status as a regional team. It operates with a modest stadium and squad, focusing mainly on local players and development rather than top-level ambitions. Although it has never reached the elite level of Bulgarian football, the club remains an important part of Radnevo’s sporting identity and its mining-town heritage.

name: FC Minyor Pernik
content:
FC Minyor Pernik is a Bulgarian football club based in the mining town of Pernik, founded in 1919 through the merger of several local clubs. The team’s identity is closely tied to the region’s coal mining industry, which is also reflected in its name “Minyor” (“Miner”). In 1952, after several reorganisations and name changes in the post-war period, the club officially adopted its current identity.

Minyor spent many seasons fluctuating between Bulgaria’s top two divisions. It first reached the top tier in the early 1950s and experienced its strongest early spell in the 1950s–1960s, including high league finishes and a Bulgarian Cup final appearance in 1958. Over the decades, the club became known as a classic “yo-yo” team, regularly moving between the first and second divisions but often remaining competitive at national level.

In modern times, Minyor Pernik has continued to experience financial instability, relegations, and restructurings, including periods of collapse and re-founding in the 2010s. Despite these difficulties, the club has repeatedly returned to professional football, most recently competing in Bulgaria’s Second League after promotions from lower divisions. Today, it remains an important symbol of Pernik’s industrial identity and local football tradition, with its home matches played at Stadion Minyor.

name: FC Chernolomets Popovo
content:
FC Chernolomets Popovo is a Bulgarian football club based in the town of Popovo, founded in 1919. The club is one of the traditional regional teams in northern Bulgaria and has spent most of its history competing in the lower tiers of the national football system. It plays its home matches at Stamo Kostov Stadium and represents the long-standing football tradition of the Popovo region.

One of the club’s most notable historical achievements came in 1946, when Chernolomets reached the final of the Bulgarian Cup (then known as the Cup of the Tsar), finishing as runners-up after losing to Levski Sofia. This remains the club’s greatest success at national level and a defining moment in its early history.

In modern times, FC Chernolomets has largely competed in the third tier of Bulgarian football, the North-East Third League, with occasional strong seasons near the top of the table. The club has also experienced reorganisations and restructurings over the years, but it continues to exist as an active regional side, maintaining its identity as one of the historic football names from Popovo.

name: Napredak Ruse
content:
Napredyk Ruse was a Bulgarian football club founded in Ruse in 1919 after splitting from SK Sava Ruse. It was one of the wealthiest and most organized clubs in the city, even owning its own pitch. The club was initially established by pharmacist Georgi Manev and wealthy merchant Stefan Nedkov, and it quickly became a key force in local football. During the 1920s it went through several mergers and name changes, becoming Botev Ruse in 1926, then Botev 27 Ruse in 1927, before restoring the Napredyk name in 1931.

In competitive football, Napredyk Ruse was a strong regional contender and regularly qualified for the Bulgarian national championship finals through the Ruse regional division. The club reached the national finals multiple times in the 1930s, with its best runs including a semi-final appearance in 1931 and several more deep runs in subsequent seasons. It also competed in the Bulgarian Cup (Tsar’s Cup) during the early 1940s, reaching the final in 1941 and the semi-finals in 1942, but never managed to win a national title.

The club ceased to exist as an independent entity on 7 December 1944, when it merged with Dobrudja Ruse as part of post-war sports reorganisations in Bulgaria. This merger led to the formation of NFD “Hristo Botev”, which was soon absorbed into Dinamo Ruse. As a result, Napredyk Ruse disappeared from the football landscape, but it remains historically significant as one of the strongest early clubs from Ruse and a frequent contender in interwar Bulgarian championships.

name: FK Sportklub Plovdiv
content:
Sportklub Plovdiv originated in 1922 with the founding of its predecessor Karadzha, which soon became part of the early football development in the Plovdiv region. The club took part in the first regional championship in 1923/24, winning the second division title. In 1926 it merged with Atletik Plovdiv to form SK Sportklub, adopting red, black, and white as its colours. Despite early progress, the club lost its playing ground in 1928 after a major earthquake in Bulgaria, and for many years it had to operate without a permanent home stadium.

In the 1930s and early 1940s, Sportklub was one of the competitive but less dominant teams in Bulgarian football, often overshadowed by stronger city rivals such as Botev Plovdiv. It gradually improved and after the introduction of the national league system in 1937, the club earned promotion to the top level, finishing 5th in one season and 8th in another before World War II disrupted competition. During the war years, Sportklub participated in reorganised national tournaments, including matches against teams from Skopje and Sofia, but did not manage to achieve major national success.

In 1945, after the end of the war, Sportklub merged with Partsjevich Plovdiv (founded in 1923) to form SP 45 Plovdiv. This new entity later became known as Lokomotiv Plovdiv in 1949, marking the end of Sportklub as an independent club. Although it never won a national championship, Sportklub played an important role in the early development of Plovdiv football and eventually became part of one of Bulgaria’s most established clubs through its merger legacy.
